titulo.texto: Hammered Copper Pectoral and Jingle Bells, Purépecha

frase_gancho.texto: A copper pectoral and bells: the metal that made kings ring.

puente_narrativo.texto: From metal we move on to daily life in the West. Look for a miniature clay house with a steeply sloped thatched roof, painted with geometric designs, with tiny figures inside or in front of it.

guion_corto.texto: This copper pectoral, about eighteen centimeters wide, and these bells, between three and six centimeters, come from Michoacán and were made by the Purépecha about seven hundred years ago. The pectoral was made from a hammered sheet of copper decorated with relief designs; the bells were made by pouring molten metal into a mold. Each one holds a small pellet inside that rings when it moves. Notice the warm gleam of the metal, which recalled the sun. The Purépecha mastered metals like few peoples of Mesoamerica: they worked copper, silver, gold, and bronze, and used them for jewelry and also for tools, such as needles and fishhooks. This piece joins art and sound: a jewel that could be heard.

guion_largo.texto:
Close your eyes and imagine a procession. A ruler walks; with every step, many copper bells jingle. Before you see him, you hear him. This is the sound of the metals of the West.

In the Oaxaca Hall you saw the [gold pectoral from Tomb 7](mna_s07_pectoral_oro_tumba7), and I told you that the technique of metalworking reached Mesoamerica from South America. Here it becomes clearer: metalworking developed first in West Mexico, where it arrived, probably by sea, from Ecuador, Peru, or Colombia, around the year seven hundred of our era. Some relate it to the [Capacha vessel](mna_s10_vasija_capacha) that you saw when you entered the hall: one and the same Pacific route, centuries apart.

The first things made were bells, tweezers, rings, and needles. Sound and shine mattered as much as value. In the Mesoamerican world, the yellow and reddish metal was associated with the Sun and with the gods. You had already seen clay bells on the [dancer from Tlatilco](mna_s03_bailarina_cascabeles); here, those same bells turn to metal.

The Purépecha took the technique further. They learned to hammer copper into sheets, to heat it so it would not crack, and to cast it, and to mix it with tin or arsenic to obtain bronze, which is harder. With this they made not only jewelry but also tools: needles, fishhooks, adzes, and T-shaped axes. It is thought that some of those axes were used as currency.

The bells were made with the lost-wax technique, the same one used for the gold pectoral from Monte Albán. The bell was modeled in wax, covered with clay, and heated until the wax melted and ran out, and into that hollow the molten metal was poured. When the mold was broken, the piece was there. Inside, a small stone or pellet was placed so that it would ring.

These bells did not stay at home. Copper bells have been found at the Templo Mayor and even at Paquimé, in the Chihuahua desert, more than a thousand kilometers from Michoacán, and it is thought that many come from the West. Copper traveled. The peoples of the north and the center valued it as much as the Purépecha produced it.

Where did the copper come from? It is thought to have come from the region of the Balsas River, between Michoacán and Guerrero: the same area the green stone of Mezcala comes from. A territory rich in materials, crossed by trade routes.

And the sound had its logic. In many cultures of Mesoamerica, bells accompanied dance and announced the presence of an important person: whoever jingled made himself noticed. Today, in Michoacán, a tradition of hand-hammered copper is still alive in the town of Santa Clara del Cobre.

In a world without iron, metal was not used only for cutting. It was used to shine, to sound, to show power. And the best proof of this is that, after so many halls of stone and clay, here appears a material that can be heard.

texto: Look at the gleam of the copper and the reliefs on the pectoral
Count the bells and compare their sizes
Imagine the sound they would make all together as someone walked

texto.Material: Native copper and bronze alloys, hammered, embossed, and cast using the lost-wax method
texto.Origin: Lake Pátzcuaro basin (Tzintzuntzan and Ihuatzio), Michoacán

texto.pregunta: Myth: Before the Spaniards, metals were unknown in Mexico.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Copper, gold, and silver had been worked for more than a thousand years, and the Purépecha were masters of the technique.
